abstract: This reflection essay argues that explanations of contemporary democratic backsliding fall into two largely separate camps—a 'technocentric' paradigm focused on disinformation and algorithmic amplification, and an 'institutionalist' paradigm focused on parties, elites, and institutions—each of which has significant blind spots. The authors propose a synthesizing framework centered on 'digitally networked organizations' that bridges the two, showing how fluid online networks are managed into party 'surrogate organizations' that radicalize conservative parties. They illustrate the argument primarily through Donald Trump and the MAGA transformation of the US Republican Party, with parallels drawn to other democracies.
key_claims: Democratic backsliding cannot be adequately explained by either individual-level media effects (technocentric) or institutional/elite dynamics (institutionalist) alone; the two must be integrated.

The missing link between the two paradigms is 'digitally networked organizations'—fluid, less hierarchical formations that connect scattered extremist individuals and fringe groups into movements, parties, and elections.

Building on Ziblatt's 'conservative dilemma,' conservative parties resolve their electoral disadvantage by mobilizing cross-cutting cultural cleavages through 'surrogate organizations,' which now increasingly include online 'digital surrogate organizations' such as QAnon, the Proud Boys, and anti-vaccine networks.

Right-wing extremist networks form more stable and coherent party-linked organizations than left-wing ones—not because of technological differences but because of fewer core values, greater aversion to hierarchy on the left, and well-resourced right-wing media and donor infrastructure.

The MAGA movement transformed the Republican Party by making party boundaries 'porous,' pulling traditional surrogates (e.g., Fox News, Christian nationalist groups) toward extremism and undermining institutional gatekeeping.
Similar combinations of institutional and communication factors are producing illiberal transformations across many democracies, indicating the framework's comparative applicability.
methods: Conceptual synthesis and critical literature review of two research traditions ('technocentric' and 'institutionalist' approaches to democratic erosion).
Theory-building extending Bennett and Segerberg's 'connective action'/'communication as organization' framework and Ziblatt's 'conservative dilemma' and 'surrogate organization' concepts.
Illustrative case analysis of the US Republican Party, MAGA movement, the 'Stop the Steal' campaign, and the January 6, 2021 Capitol attack.

Use of secondary evidence including V-Dem and Economist Democracy Index reports, the Atlantic Council DFRLab #StopTheSteal timeline, Just Security engagement data, SPLC counts of extremist organizations, and journalistic/court sources (e.g., Dominion v. Fox testimony).
Brief comparative gestures to other cases (AfD in Germany, Orbán in Hungary, Sweden, EU parliament elections).
findings: Global democracy indices show sharp declines (V-Dem: average citizen's democracy level in 2022 back to 1986 levels; the US downgraded to a 'flawed democracy' after 2016).

Individual-level cognitive research (e.g., inoculation, fact-checking, correction) has produced unstable and often non-replicable results (e.g., the 'backfire effect' failed to replicate), and generous funding (~$70M, 2016–2021) has entrenched a paradigm that elides power and institutions.

The 'Stop the Steal' meme generated over 8,200 articles and more than 70 million engagements (Sept 2020–Feb 2021), with the bulk on YouTube; belief that Biden's 2020 win was legitimate declined over time (only 61% of adults and 31% of Republicans by 2024).

Right-wing digital surrogates were enabled by five networking mechanisms: partisan media/influencers, tax-exempt nonprofits and think tanks, political operatives, elected leaders' cueing, and spreadable memes/disinformation.

Trump and Republican elites failed the 'distancing capacity' (Bermeo) needed to separate the party from violence and lawlessness, and at times actively promoted violence, accelerating illiberal transition.
Left-wing networked mobilizations (Occupy, #MeToo, #BlackLivesMatter) tend to be large but short-lived and dissolve rather than form durable party coalitions.
contributions: Offers an integrative framework linking technocentric and institutionalist explanations of democratic backsliding at the organizational (rather than individual or purely institutional) level.
Extends the concept of party 'surrogate organizations' to 'digital surrogate organizations,' clarifying how online extremist networks are incorporated into and radicalize parties.
Provides a critical appraisal of 'mis/disinformation studies,' highlighting conceptual ambiguity, replication problems, and neglect of structural power.
Explains the asymmetry between Left and Right in forming stable networked party coalitions.
Sketches a comparative agenda for studying illiberal communication spheres and transnational networking across democracies.
framing: The paper positions itself at the intersection of political communication and comparative democratization studies, bridging scholarship on disinformation and platform power with institutionalist theories of democratic backsliding (Ziblatt, Levitsky, Bermeo, Hacker and Pierson). It advances a 'communication as organization'/connective-action lens to argue that neither media effects nor party institutionalism alone can explain the rise of illiberalism.
